title: Die schöne Katrinelje und Pif Paf Poltrie
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 131. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly. The tale's closing verse (Katrinelje's dowry list) is in Low German (Plattdeutsch); the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form there.
about: KHM 131 is barely a story at all — a cumulative courtship rhyme in which the suitor Pif Paf Poltrie greets each member of fair Katrinelje's family in turn (Father Hollenthe, Mother Milk-Cow, Brother High-and-Proud, Sister Cheese-and-Curds) and asks the same question down the line, until Katrinelje herself tallies up a dowry of pocket change and dried pears, and the groom's trade turns out, after much guessing, to be nothing grander than binding brooms. The pleasure is in the repetition and the anticlimax rather than in any plot.

sentences.t: „Guten Tag, Vater Hollenthe.“ „Großen Dank, Pif Paf Poltrie.“
sentences.l: “Good day, Father Hollenthe.” “Great thanks, Pif Paf Poltrie.”
sentences.i: “Good day to you, Father Hollenthe.” “Many thanks, Pif Paf Poltrie.”
sentences.n: The tale opens straight into speech and never leaves it: there is no narrator anywhere in it. “Großen Dank” is the old set reply to a greeting — you thank the other for greeting you. Every name here means something, and the glossary is where you will find each one.

sentences.t: „Könnt ich wohl eure Tochter kriegen?“ „O ja, wenns die Mutter Malcho (Melk-Kuh), der Bruder Hohenstolz, die Schwester Käsetraut und die schöne Katrinelje will, so kanns geschehen.“
sentences.l: “Could I indeed get your daughter?” “Oh yes, if the mother Malcho (milk-cow), the brother Hohenstolz, the sister Käsetraut and the fair Katrinelje are willing, then it can come about.”
sentences.i: “Might I have your daughter?” “Oh yes — if Mother Malcho (the milk-cow), Brother Hohenstolz, Sister Käsetraut and fair Katrinelje are willing, then it can be done.”
sentences.n: The round brackets around “(Melk-Kuh)” are the Grimms’ own: they printed the gloss in the 1857 text to tell their readers what the name Malcho means. Nothing here has been supplied by this edition. “wenns” is wenn es and “kanns” is kann es, run together as in speech; “kriegen” has its plain old sense, to get. The father sends the suitor on to the next of kin, and that sending-on is the whole tale.

sentences.t:
„Wo ist dann die Mutter Malcho?“
„Sie ist im Stall und melkt die Kuh.“
sentences.l:
“Where then is the mother Malcho?”
“She is in the stall and milks the cow.”
sentences.i:
“And where is Mother Malcho?”
“She is in the byre, milking the cow.”
sentences.n: The first of five rhymed couplets. The German pairs Malcho with Kuh — a loose rhyme, and the reason the answer has to name a chore. Lectorium’s idiomatic line does not rhyme; the German does the rhyming. “dann” here is the spoken form of denn, the little particle that colours a question: well then, where…

sentences.t: „Guten Tag, Mutter Malcho.“ „Großen Dank, Pif Paf Poltrie.“
sentences.l: “Good day, Mother Malcho.” “Great thanks, Pif Paf Poltrie.”
sentences.i: “Good day to you, Mother Malcho.” “Many thanks, Pif Paf Poltrie.”
sentences.n: The greeting comes back word for word with only the name changed — the repetition is the form of the tale, not an accident of it.

sentences.t: „Könnt ich wohl eure Tochter kriegen?“ „O ja, wenns der Vater Hollenthe, der Bruder Hohenstolz, die Schwester Käsetraut und die schöne Katrinelje will, so kanns geschehen.“
sentences.l: “Could I indeed get your daughter?” “Oh yes, if the father Hollenthe, the brother Hohenstolz, the sister Käsetraut and the fair Katrinelje are willing, then it can come about.”
sentences.i: “Might I have your daughter?” “Oh yes — if Father Hollenthe, Brother Hohenstolz, Sister Käsetraut and fair Katrinelje are willing, then it can be done.”
sentences.n: The list is the same as the father’s, with one swap: whoever is being asked drops out of it, and the one already asked takes their place. Nobody ever says no, and nobody ever says yes. The verb stays singular — will, not wollen — though four people are named: the old loose agreement takes the list as one block.

sentences.t:
„Wo ist dann der Bruder Hohenstolz?“
„Er ist in der Kammer und hackt das Holz.“
sentences.l:
“Where then is the brother Hohenstolz?”
“He is in the chamber and chops the wood.”
sentences.i:
“And where is Brother Hohenstolz?”
“He is in the chamber, chopping wood.”
sentences.n: Hohenstolz / Holz is a full rhyme this time. die Kammer is any small room of the house — a chamber, not a bedroom in the modern sense.

sentences.t: „Guten Tag, Bruder Hohenstolz.“ „Großen Dank, Pif Paf Poltrie.“
sentences.l: “Good day, Brother Hohenstolz.” “Great thanks, Pif Paf Poltrie.”
sentences.i: “Good day to you, Brother Hohenstolz.” “Many thanks, Pif Paf Poltrie.”
sentences.n: Third time, same greeting.

sentences.t: „Könnt ich wohl eure Schwester kriegen?“ „O ja, wenns der Vater Hollenthe, die Mutter Malcho, die Schwester Käsetraut und die schöne Katrinelje will, so kanns geschehen.“
sentences.l: “Could I indeed get your sister?” “Oh yes, if the father Hollenthe, the mother Malcho, the sister Käsetraut and the fair Katrinelje are willing, then it can come about.”
sentences.i: “Might I have your sister?” “Oh yes — if Father Hollenthe, Mother Malcho, Sister Käsetraut and fair Katrinelje are willing, then it can be done.”
sentences.n: The question shifts from Tochter to Schwester now that he is asking a brother; the answer keeps its shape.

sentences.t:
„Wo ist dann die Schwester Käsetraut?“
„Sie ist im Garten und schneidet das Kraut.“
sentences.l:
“Where then is the sister Käsetraut?”
“She is in the garden and cuts the greens.”
sentences.i:
“And where is Sister Käsetraut?”
“She is in the garden, cutting the greens.”
sentences.n: Käsetraut / Kraut is the rhyme, and it is also where her name came from: das Kraut is the leafy green stuff of the kitchen garden — cabbage, herbs, greens.

sentences.t: „Guten Tag, Schwester Käsetraut.“ „Großen Dank, Pif Paf Poltrie.“
sentences.l: “Good day, Sister Käsetraut.” “Great thanks, Pif Paf Poltrie.”
sentences.i: “Good day to you, Sister Käsetraut.” “Many thanks, Pif Paf Poltrie.”
sentences.n: Fourth time; only the name moves.

sentences.t: „Könnt ich wohl eure Schwester kriegen?“ „O ja, wenns der Vater Hollenthe, die Mutter Malcho, der Bruder Hohenstolz und die schöne Katrinelje will, so kanns geschehen.“
sentences.l: “Could I indeed get your sister?” “Oh yes, if the father Hollenthe, the mother Malcho, the brother Hohenstolz and the fair Katrinelje are willing, then it can come about.”
sentences.i: “Might I have your sister?” “Oh yes — if Father Hollenthe, Mother Malcho, Brother Hohenstolz and fair Katrinelje are willing, then it can be done.”
sentences.n: Only Katrinelje herself is left unasked, and she comes next.

sentences.t:
„Wo ist dann die schöne Katrinelje?“
„Sie ist in der Kammer und zählt ihre Pfennige.“
sentences.l:
“Where then is the fair Katrinelje?”
“She is in the chamber and counts her pennies.”
sentences.i:
“And where is fair Katrinelje?”
“She is in the chamber, counting her pennies.”
sentences.n: Katrinelje / Pfennige is the loosest of the five rhymes — it chimes rather than rhymes. Counting her pennies is the first hint of what her dowry will turn out to be.

sentences.t: „Guten Tag, schöne Katrinelje.“ „Großen Dank, Pif Paf Poltrie.“
sentences.l: “Good day, fair Katrinelje.” “Great thanks, Pif Paf Poltrie.”
sentences.i: “Good day to you, fair Katrinelje.” “Many thanks, Pif Paf Poltrie.”
sentences.n: Fifth and last time.

sentences.t: „Willst du wohl mein Schatz sein?“ „O ja, wenns der Vater Hollenthe, die Mutter Malcho, der Bruder Hohenstolz, die Schwester Käsetraut will, so kanns geschehen.“
sentences.l: “Will you indeed be my treasure?” “Oh yes, if the father Hollenthe, the mother Malcho, the brother Hohenstolz, the sister Käsetraut are willing, then it can come about.”
sentences.i: “Will you be my sweetheart?” “Oh yes — if Father Hollenthe, Mother Malcho, Brother Hohenstolz and Sister Käsetraut are willing, then it can be done.”
sentences.n: The question changes at last: to her he says “mein Schatz” — Schatz is a treasure, and used of a person it is a sweetheart, still the ordinary German endearment today. Her answer names the other four and leaves herself out, so the circle closes with nobody having decided anything.

sentences.t: „Schön Katrinelje, wie viel hast du an Brautschatz?“
sentences.l: “Fair Katrinelje, how much have you in bride-treasure?”
sentences.i: “Fair Katrinelje, how much do you have by way of a dowry?”
sentences.n: “Schön” stands here without its ending, an old vocative use kept in songs and tales. der Brautschatz is what the bride brings into the marriage — literally her bride-treasure. With the courting settled, the accounting begins.

sentences.t: „Vierzehn Pfennige baares Geld, drittehalb Groschen Schuld, ein halb Pfund Hutzeln, eine Hand voll Prutzeln, eine Hand voll Wurzelen,
sentences.l: “Fourteen pennies ready money, two-and-a-half groschen of debt, a half pound of dried pears, a hand full of cracklings, a hand full of roots,
sentences.i: “Fourteen pence in ready money, two and a half groschen of debt, half a pound of dried pears, a handful of cracklings, a handful of roots,
sentences.n: The joke is the smallness of it, recited with the gravity of an inventory — and one item is a debt. “baares Geld” (modern bares Geld) is money in hand. “drittehalb” is the old way of saying two and a half: you count to the third and take only half of it, as anderthalb is one and a half. Hutzeln are dried pears; Prutzeln are fried scraps, and the word is regional enough that its exact sense is uncertain. The sentence breaks off with a comma and runs straight on into the verse.

sentences.t:
un so der watt:
is dat nig en guden Brutschatt?“
sentences.l:
and so on and such:
is that not a good bride-treasure?”
sentences.i:
and so forth and such-like:
is that not a good dowry?”
sentences.n: The tale drops into Low German (Plattdeutsch) for its last two lines — the punchline lands in dialect, and the switch is the joke’s delivery. dat = das, nig = nicht, en = ein, guden = guten, Brutschatt = Brautschatz. “un so der watt” is a set phrase of the “and such-like” sort; its word-for-word sense is not really recoverable, and the rendering above is a reading, not a certainty. The German rhymes watt / Brutschatt.

sentences.t: „Pif Paf Poltrie, was kannst du für ein Handwerk? bist du ein Schneider?“ „Noch viel besser.“
sentences.l: “Pif Paf Poltrie, what trade can you? are you a tailor?” “Better still by far.”
sentences.i: “Pif Paf Poltrie, what trade do you follow? Are you a tailor?” “Far better than that.”
sentences.n: “was kannst du für ein Handwerk” — können with a trade as its object means to have it at your fingertips, to have learnt it; English has to put in a verb like follow or know. “Noch viel besser” is the answer he will give to every guess, and the tale is now a second chain, of trades instead of kin.

sentences.t: „Ein Schuster?“ „Noch viel besser.“
sentences.l: “A shoemaker?” “Better still by far.”
sentences.i: “A cobbler?” “Far better than that.”
sentences.n: Second guess, same answer.

sentences.t: „Ein Ackersmann?“ „Noch viel besser.“
sentences.l: “A ploughman?” “Better still by far.”
sentences.i: “A husbandman?” “Far better than that.”
sentences.n: der Ackersmann is the man who works the Acker, the ploughland — an old word where modern German would say Bauer.

sentences.t: „Ein Schreiner?“ „Noch viel besser.“
sentences.l: “A joiner?” “Better still by far.”
sentences.i: “A cabinetmaker?” “Far better than that.”
sentences.n: der Schreiner is the joiner, who works finished wood, as against the Zimmermann who frames houses.

sentences.t: „Ein Schmied?“ „Noch viel besser.“
sentences.l: “A smith?” “Better still by far.”
sentences.i: “A blacksmith?” “Far better than that.”
sentences.n: Fifth guess; she is naming the trades of a village one after another.

sentences.t: „Ein Müller?“ „Noch viel besser.“
sentences.l: “A miller?” “Better still by far.”
sentences.i: “A miller?” “Far better than that.”
sentences.n: Sixth, and the last of the solid trades she can think of.

sentences.t: „Vielleicht ein Besenbinder?“ „Ja, das bin ich: ist das nicht ein schönes Handwerk?“
sentences.l: “Perhaps a broom-binder?” “Yes, that I am: is that not a fine trade?”
sentences.i: “Perhaps a broom-maker?” “Yes, that is what I am — is that not a fine trade?”
sentences.n: It ends on the poorest craft of all: a Besenbinder ties birch twigs into brooms, and needs neither shop nor stock to do it. He is delighted with it, and asks a question nobody answers — a dowry of fourteen pennies and a debt has found its match. “Vielleicht” carries her dwindling hope.

glossary.an: an — at, on, against; of an amount, in the way of (“wie viel hast du an Brautschatz?” = how much do you have by way of a dowry?)
glossary.dann: dann — then; here the spoken form of denn, the particle that colours a question (“wo ist dann …?” = well, where is …?)
glossary.geschehen: geschehen — to happen, to come about (infinitive; “so kanns geschehen” = then it can come about)
glossary.großen: groß — great, big (adj., inflected; “Großen Dank” = many thanks, the old set reply to a greeting)
glossary.ja: ja — yes (“O ja” = oh yes); also a particle, surely, after all
glossary.könnt: können — could (1st sg. subjunctive, old short form of könnte: “könnt ich” = could I)
glossary.schatz: der Schatz — treasure; and as a term of endearment, sweetheart (“mein Schatz sein” = to be my sweetheart)
glossary.schuld: die Schuld — debt, money owed; also fault, blame
